This is a fascinating project - building a machine to play Guitar Hero automatically. Let me think through the key aspects and questions I need to ask to create a good specification.

Key components of such a system:
1. **Vision System** - Capture and process the game screen to detect:
   - Which notes are coming (colors: green, red, yellow, blue, orange)
   - When to press them (timing based on position)
   - Star power opportunities
   - Possibly whammy bar for held notes

2. **Hardware Controller Interface** - Actuate the guitar controller:
   - 5 fret buttons
   - Strum bar (up/down)
   - Possibly whammy bar
   - Star power tilt sensor

3. **Processing/Control Unit** - Bridge between vision and actuation:
   - Could be a PC doing vision + sending commands to microcontroller
   - Or embedded system doing everything
   - Real-time timing is critical

4. **Timing & Latency** - Guitar Hero is timing-sensitive:
   - Need to account for video capture latency
   - Processing latency
   - Actuation latency

Questions I should ask:

1. **Target platform**: Which Guitar Hero game and console? (PS2, PS3, Xbox 360, Wii, Clone Hero on PC?) This affects:
   - Video capture method
   - Controller interface type
   - Game speed/mechanics

2. **Controller approach**: 
   - Modify an existing guitar controller with solenoids/servos?
   - Build a custom controller that emulates the protocol?
   - Use a PC-based game (Clone Hero) with software input?

3. **Processing architecture**:
   - PC for vision + microcontroller (PIC?) for actuation?
   - All-in-one embedded solution?
   - What's the "PIC" in the folder name referring to?

4. **Video capture method**:
   - HDMI capture card?
   - Camera pointed at screen?
   - Direct frame buffer access (if PC game)?

5. **Performance goals**:
   - What difficulty level? (Easy through Expert)
   - What accuracy target?
   - Speed (songs can go 200+ notes per second on expert)

6. **Scope**:
   - Just hit notes? 
   - Star power management?
   - Whammy bar for sustained notes?

I need to ask the most critical questions first to understand the constraints and shape the overall approach.</details></think>

```json
{
  "name": "Guitar Hero Bot Spec",
  "overview": "Create a comprehensive specification document for an autonomous Guitar Hero playing machine that uses computer vision to observe a PS2 game, processes notes in real-time, and mechanically actuates a physical guitar controller via PIC microcontroller.",
  "plan": "# Guitar Hero Bot Specification Document\n\n## Project Overview\n\nBuild an autonomous system that plays Guitar Hero on PS2 by:\n1. Capturing and analyzing video output from PS2\n2. Detecting note patterns, timing, and game state via computer vision\n3. Mechanically actuating a real guitar controller using solenoids/servos\n4. Coordinating timing via PIC microcontroller\n\n**Target**: Start with Easy difficulty, design architecture to scale to Expert with full features (notes, star power, whammy).\n\n---\n\n## System Architecture\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;mermaid\nflowchart LR\n    subgraph console [PS2 Console]\n        GH[Guitar Hero Game]\n    end\n    \n    subgraph vision [Vision System]\n        VC[Video Capture Device]\n        PC[PC/SBC Processing]\n    end\n    \n    subgraph control [Control System]\n        PIC[PIC Microcontroller]\n        DRV[Motor Drivers]\n    end\n    \n    subgraph mechanical [Mechanical Actuators]\n        SOL[Solenoids x5 Frets]\n        STR[Strum Actuator]\n        WHM[Whammy Servo]\n        TLT[Tilt Mechanism]\n    end\n    \n    subgraph guitar [Guitar Controller]\n        CTRL[PS2 Guitar]\n    end\n    \n    GH --\u003e|Video Out| VC\n    VC --\u003e|USB| PC\n    PC --\u003e|Serial/USB| PIC\n    PIC --\u003e DRV\n    DRV --\u003e SOL\n    DRV --\u003e STR\n    DRV --\u003e WHM\n    DRV --\u003e TLT\n    SOL --\u003e CTRL\n    STR --\u003e CTRL\n    WHM --\u003e CTRL\n    TLT --\u003e CTRL\n    CTRL --\u003e|Controller Port| GH\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n---\n\n## Hardware Subsystems\n\n### 1. Video Capture Options\n\n| Method | Pros | Cons |\n|--------|------|------|\n| **Composite capture** (EasyCap, etc.) | Cheap ($10-20), simple | Low resolution (480i), latency varies |\n| **Component capture** (Elgato, AverMedia) | Better quality (480p) | More expensive ($50-150) |\n| **Camera on screen** | No cable modification | Lighting issues, calibration needed |\n\n**Recommendation**: Start with composite capture for simplicity; upgrade to component if resolution is limiting.\n\n### 2. PIC Microcontroller Requirements\n\n- **Timing precision**: Sub-millisecond control for note accuracy\n- **I/O pins needed**: Minimum 8 (5 frets + strum up/down + whammy PWM)\n- **Communication**: UART or USB to host PC\n- **Suggested families**: PIC18F or PIC24F series\n\n### 3. Mechanical Actuation\n\n**Fret Buttons (x5)**:\n- Small push-pull solenoids (5-12V, ~10-20ms response)\n- Or micro servos with lever mechanism\n- Mount above each fret button\n\n**Strum Bar**:\n- Bidirectional actuation (up and down strum)\n- Solenoid pair or rotary servo\n- Must support rapid alternating strums (up to 10+ Hz on Expert)\n\n**Whammy Bar**:\n- Servo motor with 90-degree range\n- Continuous oscillation during sustained notes\n\n**Star Power Tilt**:\n- Servo or motor to tilt the entire guitar\n- Or accelerometer sensor bypass (tap into controller circuit)\n\n---\n\n## Software Subsystems\n\n### 1. Vision Processing (PC/SBC)\n\n**Platform options**: Python + OpenCV, or C++ for lower latency\n\n**Detection requirements**:\n- **Note highway tracking**: Identify the 5 lanes (green, red, yellow, blue, orange)\n- **Note detection**: Colored circles/gems approaching strike line\n- **Timing calculation**: Distance from note to strike line → time to hit\n- **Chord detection**: Multiple simultaneous notes\n- **Sustain detection**: Long notes requiring hold\n- **Star Power phrases**: Glowing note sequences\n- **Star Power meter**: When to activate\n\n**Frame rate target**: 30-60 FPS processing to match game output\n\n### 2. Note Scheduling and Timing\n\n- Build a queue of upcoming notes with predicted hit times\n- Account for total system latency:\n  - Video capture latency (~30-100ms)\n  - Processing latency (~10-30ms)  \n  - Serial communication (~1-5ms)\n  - Solenoid actuation (~10-20ms)\n- Calibration routine to measure and compensate for latency\n\n### 3. PIC Firmware\n\n- Receive note commands via serial (fret mask + strum direction + timing offset)\n- Precise timer-based actuation\n- PWM control for whammy servo\n- Tilt activation on command\n\n---\n\n## Communication Protocol\n\nPC to PIC serial commands (example format):\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n[CMD][FRETS][STRUM][TIMING_MS]\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n- &#96;CMD&#96;: Note (0x01), Strum (0x02), Whammy (0x03), Tilt (0x04)\n- &#96;FRETS&#96;: Bitmask (bit 0=green, bit 4=orange)\n- &#96;STRUM&#96;: 0=none, 1=down, 2=up\n- &#96;TIMING_MS&#96;: Milliseconds until actuation (0 = immediate)\n\n---\n\n## Development Phases\n\n### Phase 1: Foundation\n- Set up video capture pipeline\n- Basic note detection (single notes, one color)\n- PIC firmware with single solenoid test\n- End-to-end proof of concept on Easy difficulty\n\n### Phase 2: Core Gameplay\n- Full 5-fret detection and actuation\n- Chord detection\n- Strum timing calibration\n- Play through Easy songs reliably\n\n### Phase 3: Advanced Features\n- Sustain note detection + whammy actuation\n- Star Power phrase detection\n- Star Power activation (tilt mechanism)\n- Medium/Hard difficulty support\n\n### Phase 4: Expert Mode\n- Fast strum patterns (alt-strumming logic)\n- Sub-frame timing optimization\n- Full Expert song completion\n\n---\n\n## File Structure\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nguitar-pic/\n├── SPEC.md                    # This specification document\n├── docs/\n│   ├── hardware-bom.md        # Bill of materials\n│   ├── wiring-diagram.md      # Connection schematics\n│   └── calibration.md         # Timing calibration guide\n├── vision/\n│   ├── requirements.txt       # _**Agent (claude-4.5-opus-high-thinking)**_
```

Here's a detailed breakdown of your video capture options for the PS2:

## PS2 Video Output Types

The PS2 can output video in several formats (from lowest to highest quality):

| Output | Resolution | Cable Type | Quality |
|--------|-----------|------------|---------|
| **RF** | 240p-480i | Coax to TV | Worst (don't use) |
| **Composite** | 480i | Yellow RCA | Poor but usable |
| **S-Video** | 480i | 4-pin mini-DIN | Better than composite |
| **Component** | 480p | Red/Green/Blue RCA | Best for PS2 |

---

## Option 1: Composite/S-Video USB Capture (Recommended to Start)

**Examples**: EasyCap, Elgato Video Capture, Dazzle

```
PS2 ──[Composite/S-Video]──► USB Capture Dongle ──► PC
```

**Pros**:
- Cheap ($10-25)
- Simple plug-and-play
- Works with standard PS2 AV cable you already have
- Plenty of Linux/Mac/Windows driver support

**Cons**:
- 480i interlaced (some frame artifacts)
- Latency varies by device (30-100ms)
- Cheap clones can have inconsistent quality

**Recommended devices**:
- **EasyCap clones** (~$10) - Hit or miss quality, but cheap to try
- **Elgato Video Capture** (~$50) - More reliable, better drivers
- **StarTech SVID2USB** (~$40) - Good Linux support

**Latency note**: The capture latency doesn't affect gameplay (since we're compensating for it), but it does affect how far ahead we can "see" notes.

---

## Option 2: Component Video Capture

**Examples**: Elgato Game Capture HD, AverMedia, Datapath

```
PS2 ──[Component cables]──► Component Capture ──► PC
```

**Pros**:
- 480p progressive (no interlacing artifacts)
- Cleaner image for note detection
- Lower latency on good devices (20-50ms)

**Cons**:
- More expensive ($50-150)
- Requires PS2 component cables ($10-20 extra)
- Some devices are HDCP sensitive (less of an issue for PS2)

**Recommended devices**:
- **Elgato Game Capture HD** (~$100 used) - Solid, well-supported
- **AverMedia Live Gamer** (~$80-150) - Low latency options
- **RetroTINK + HDMI capture** (~$150 total) - Converts to HDMI first

---

## Option 3: Camera Pointed at Screen

```
PS2 ──► TV ◄── Camera ──► PC
```

**Pros**:
- No cable modifications
- Works with any display
- Can capture CRT (authentic experience)

**Cons**:
- Requires camera positioning/mounting
- Lighting affects detection reliability
- Need to calibrate for screen geometry
- Potential for glare, reflections
- Additional latency from TV display

**If going this route**:
- Use a USB webcam with manual exposure control
- 60fps capability helps
- Mount camera directly above/below screen
- Control ambient lighting

---

## Option 4: Upscaler + HDMI Capture

```
PS2 ──[Component]──► RetroTINK/OSSC ──[HDMI]──► HDMI Capture ──► PC
```

**Pros**:
- Best image quality
- Can use modern HDMI capture cards
- RetroTINK adds minimal latency (~1 frame)
- Future-proof for other retro consoles

**Cons**:
- Most expensive ($150-250 total)
- More points of failure
- Overkill for this project

---

## My Recommendation

**Start with a cheap composite capture** (~$15 EasyCap or similar):

1. It's the fastest way to get frames into your PC
2. 480i is actually fine for note detection (notes are large, colorful)
3. Latency can be calibrated out
4. If it works, you've saved money
5. If detection struggles, upgrade to component later

**Test before buying expensive gear** - The vision system needs to detect:
- 5 distinct colors (easy even at 480i)
- Position on screen (easy)
- Movement between frames (easy)

The hard part is timing, not image quality.

---

## Quick Test Setup

Once you have a capture device:

```bash
# List video devices
python vision/main.py --list-devices

# Test capture with debug display
python vision/main.py -d -v 0  # Try device 0, 1, 2...
```

_**Agent (claude-4.5-opus-high-thinking)**_

The Elgato Game Capture HD connects via **USB 2.0** to your PC. Here's the full signal chain:

```
┌─────────┐    Component Cables     ┌──────────────────────┐    USB 2.0    ┌─────────┐
│   PS2   │ ───────────────────────►│  Elgato Game         │ ─────────────►│   PC    │
│         │   (Red/Green/Blue +     │  Capture HD          │               │         │
│         │    Red/White Audio)     │                      │               │         │
└─────────┘                         └──────────────────────┘               └─────────┘
```

## What You'll Need

| Item | Purpose | Est. Cost |
|------|---------|-----------|
| **PS2 Component Cables** | Video from PS2 | $10-20 |
| **Elgato Game Capture HD** | Capture device | $50-80 used |
| **USB 2.0 cable** | Included with Elgato | - |

## Elgato Game Capture HD Ports

```
Front:                          Back:
┌─────────────────────┐        ┌─────────────────────────────────┐
│  [HDMI IN]          │        │  [USB 2.0]  [POWER]             │
│  [HDMI OUT]         │        │                                 │
│  [Component IN]─────┼────────│◄── You'll use this              │
│  [Analog Audio IN]  │        │                                 │
│  [AV IN adapter]    │        │                                 │
└─────────────────────┘        └─────────────────────────────────┘
```

## Connection Steps

1. **PS2 Component Cable** → Plug the 5 RCA ends into Elgato:
   - Green (Y) → Green input
   - Blue (Pb) → Blue input  
   - Red (Pr) → Red input
   - Red (audio R) → Red audio input
   - White (audio L) → White audio input

2. **USB Cable** → Elgato to PC (any USB 2.0 or 3.0 port)

3. **Power** → Elgato comes with a power adapter (it's not bus-powered)

## Software Access

The Elgato appears as a standard video capture device. You can access it with:

**OpenCV (what our vision system uses)**:
```python
import cv2
cap = cv2.VideoCapture(0)  # or 1, 2 depending on device index
```

**Test with our code**:
```bash
python vision/main.py --list-devices
python vision/main.py -d -v 1  # try different numbers
```

**Elgato's own software** (optional, for testing):
- Elgato Game Capture software (Windows/Mac)
- Can verify signal is working before using OpenCV

## Expected Specs with This Setup

| Metric | Value |
|--------|-------|
| Resolution | 480p (progressive) |
| Frame rate | 60fps from PS2, captured at 30/60 |
| Latency | ~40-60ms (capture only) |
| Color quality | Good - clean for note detection |

## One Note on PS2 Component

Make sure to enable **progressive scan (480p)** in Guitar Hero's options if available, or in the PS2 system settings. Some PS2 games default to 480i even over component. Guitar Hero should support 480p which will give you cleaner frames.

_**Agent (claude-4.5-opus-high-thinking)**_

No, the Elgato Game Capture HD is a **mid-range option** for latency. Here's how it compares:

## Capture Device Latency Comparison

| Device | Connection | Latency | Cost | Notes |
|--------|------------|---------|------|-------|
| **Datapath VisionRGB** | PCIe | ~5-10ms | $300-500 | Professional, lowest |
| **Magewell Pro Capture** | PCIe | ~10-15ms | $300-400 | Excellent quality |
| **Blackmagic Intensity** | PCIe/Thunderbolt | ~15-30ms | $150-250 | Good balance |
| **AverMedia Live Gamer 4K** | PCIe | ~15-20ms | $150-200 | Gaming-focused |
| **Elgato HD60 S+** | USB 3.0 | ~30-40ms | $120-150 | Better than HD |
| **Elgato Game Capture HD** | USB 2.0 | ~50-70ms | $50-80 | What you're considering |
| **Cheap USB composite** | USB 2.0 | ~80-120ms | $10-20 | Highest latency |

## Lowest Latency Options for PS2

**Best overall: PCIe capture card with component input**

```
PS2 ──[Component]──► Blackmagic Intensity Pro ──[PCIe]──► PC
                     (~20ms latency, ~$150 used)
```

**Best USB option: AverMedia or Elgato USB 3.0 devices**

```
PS2 ──[Component]──► Elgato HD60 S+ ──[USB 3.0]──► PC
                     (~35ms latency, ~$130)
```

## Does Latency Actually Matter for This Project?

**Surprisingly, not that much.** Here's why:

1. **We compensate for it** - The vision system measures total latency and sends commands early
2. **Consistency matters more** - A stable 60ms is better than variable 20-80ms
3. **The bottleneck is elsewhere** - Solenoid actuation (~15ms) and vision processing (~20ms) add up too

**Where low latency helps:**
- Seeing notes further in advance (more reaction time margin)
- Faster scroll speeds on Expert difficulty
- Less total system delay to compensate for

## My Recommendation

| Budget | Choice | Why |
|--------|--------|-----|
| **Tight ($50-80)** | Elgato Game Capture HD | Good enough, proven |
| **Medium ($120-150)** | Elgato HD60 S+ or Blackmagic Intensity | Lower latency, USB 3.0/PCIe |
| **Best performance ($200+)** | Magewell or Datapath | Minimal latency, overkill |

For a first build, the **Elgato Game Capture HD is fine**. The ~50-70ms latency means you're seeing notes about 2-3 frames "late" - but since notes are visible for several seconds before they reach the strike line, this is easily compensated.

If you find the system struggling on Expert (very fast note sequences), upgrading the capture card would be one optimization path.

Want me to proceed with the Elgato HD, or would you prefer to look at lower-latency PCIe options?

For this Guitar Hero note detection at 30fps, the processing requirements are quite modest. Here's the breakdown:

## Per-Frame Processing Load

| Operation | Time (typical) | Notes |
|-----------|----------------|-------|
| Frame capture | ~1-2ms | OpenCV VideoCapture |
| Color conversion (BGR→HSV) | ~1-2ms | 480p frame |
| Color masking (x5 colors) | ~2-5ms | cv2.inRange per color |
| Morphological ops | ~1-2ms | Opening/closing |
| Contour detection | ~1-3ms | cv2.findContours |
| Position math | <1ms | Simple calculations |
| **Total per frame** | **~8-15ms** | Leaves plenty of headroom |

**At 30fps you have 33ms per frame** - this should use only 25-45% of that budget.

## Hardware Requirements

| Level | CPU | RAM | Works? |
|-------|-----|-----|--------|
| **Minimum** | Any dual-core from 2015+ | 4GB | Yes |
| **Comfortable** | Intel i3/i5 or Ryzen 3/5 | 8GB | Easily |
| **Raspberry Pi 4** | 4-core ARM @ 1.5GHz | 4GB | Yes, but tighter margin |
| **Raspberry Pi 3** | 4-core ARM @ 1.2GHz | 1GB | Possible, may need optimization |

## Real-World Examples

```
MacBook Air M1:        ~3-5ms per frame   (10-15% CPU)
Intel i5-8250U:        ~8-12ms per frame  (25-35% CPU)  
Raspberry Pi 4:        ~15-25ms per frame (45-75% CPU)
Raspberry Pi 3:        ~25-40ms per frame (borderline)
```

## Why It's Not Heavy

1. **Small frame size**: 480p = 640×480 = 307,200 pixels (tiny by modern standards)
2. **Simple operations**: Color thresholding is just per-pixel comparison
3. **Limited ROI**: We only process the highway region (~40% of frame)
4. **No ML/neural networks**: Just classical CV operations

## If You Need to Optimize

These changes can cut processing time significantly:

```python
# 1. Process only the highway region (already in our code)
highway_frame = frame[y_top:y_strike, x_start:x_end]  # ~40% of pixels

# 2. Resize if needed (probably unnecessary)
small = cv2.resize(frame, (320, 240))  # 4x fewer pixels

# 3. Skip frames if ahead of schedule
if time_budget_remaining > 10:
    process_frame()
```

## Bottom Line

**Any modern laptop or desktop will handle this easily.** A Raspberry Pi 4 would also work for a standalone embedded solution. The Elgato capture and USB serial will be the bottlenecks long before CPU becomes an issue.

This is a great question - RC servos have significant speed limitations that could be a problem. Let me break it down:

## RC Servo Speed Specs

| Servo | Speed (60°) | Speed (per degree) |

**For a button press** (10-15° movement): **15-40ms one way**

## Guitar Hero Timing Requirements

| Difficulty | Max Note Rate | Time Between Notes | Servo OK? |
|------------|---------------|-------------------|-----------|
| Easy | ~3 notes/sec | 333ms | Yes |
| Medium | ~5 notes/sec | 200ms | Yes |
| Hard | ~8 notes/sec | 125ms | Maybe |
| Expert | ~12-15 notes/sec | 65-80ms | No |

**Expert fast runs require <80ms per note cycle** - standard servos can't keep up.

## Solenoids vs Servos Comparison

| Factor | Solenoid | RC Servo |
|--------|----------|----------|
| **Response time** | 5-15ms | 30-80ms |
| **Cycle time** | 15-30ms | 60-150ms |
| **Max rate** | 30+ Hz | 7-15 Hz |
| **Expert difficulty** | Yes | Struggles |
| **Power consumption** | High (when active) | Low (holding) |
| **Noise** | Clicky | Quiet |
| **Control** | On/off simple | PWM position |
| **Cost** | $3-5 each | $2-5 each |

## Where Each Makes Sense

```
FRET BUTTONS:  Solenoids ✓
               - Need rapid press/release
               - On/off actuation (no position control needed)
               - 5 required

STRUM BAR:     Solenoids ✓✓ (critical path!)
               - Fastest element - up to 15 Hz alternating
               - Must be snappy for alt-strumming
               - 2 required (up + down)

WHAMMY BAR:    Servo ✓
               - Slow oscillation (1-5 Hz)
               - Position control useful
               - Not time-critical

TILT:          Servo ✓
               - One-time activation
               - Hold position
               - Not time-critical
```

## My Recommendation

**Stick with the current design:**
- **Solenoids** for frets (×5) and strum (×2) - speed critical
- **Servos** for whammy (×1) and tilt (×1) - position control, not speed critical

## If You Really Want All Servos

You could use servos for frets on Easy/Medium, but you'd need:

1. **High-speed digital servos** (~$15-25 each)
   - Example: Savox SH-0257MG (50ms/60°)
   
2. **Minimal travel** - tune for smallest movement that registers
   
3. **Accept Expert limitations** - may miss fast runs

**But honestly, solenoids are simpler and cheaper for button actuation.** The current BOM has 7 solenoids at ~$5 each ($35 total) which is comparable to 7 cheap servos and much faster.

_**Agent (claude-4.5-opus-high-thinking)**_

Good concern - solenoids can be quite clicky! Here are alternative actuator options:

## Actuator Comparison for Button Pressing

| Actuator | Speed | Noise | Cost | Complexity |
|----------|-------|-------|------|------------|
| **Solenoids** | 10-20ms | Loud click | $3-5 | Low |
| **Voice coil actuators** | 5-15ms | Quiet | $10-30 | Medium |
| **Linear servos** | 30-50ms | Quiet hum | $15-40 | Low |
| **Piezoelectric** | <1ms | Silent | $20-50 | High |
| **DC motor + cam** | 20-40ms | Motor whir | $5-10 | High |
| **Electronic bypass** | <1ms | **Silent** | $0-5 | Medium |

---

## Option 1: Voice Coil Actuators (VCA)

Like a speaker - uses magnetic coil to push/pull linearly. Used in hard drive heads.

**Pros:**
- Very fast (5-15ms)
- Quiet - no mechanical impact
- Proportional force control

**Cons:**
- Harder to source
- Need current control, not just on/off
- More expensive ($15-30 each)

**Sources:** Mouser, Digikey, salvaged from old hard drives

---

## Option 2: Quiet Solenoids with Dampening

Reduce noise by adding soft landing.

```
Standard:     Plunger ──► Hard stop ──► CLICK!

Dampened:     Plunger ──► Rubber pad ──► soft thud
              + Felt/foam around body
              + Rubber O-ring on shaft
```

**Cost:** Add ~$1-2 per solenoid in materials

**Effectiveness:** Reduces noise by 50-70%

---

## Option 3: Electronic Bypass (Recommended for Silence)

**Skip mechanical actuation entirely** - tap into the controller's button circuit.

```
Instead of:   Solenoid ──► Presses physical button ──► Closes switch

Do this:      PIC GPIO ──► Optocoupler/Transistor ──► Controller PCB
              (electrically triggers the button signal)
```

### How It Works:

1. Open the PS2 guitar controller
2. Find the button contact points on the PCB
3. Solder wires to each button's two contacts
4. Use optocouplers or transistors to "close" the circuit electronically

```
           +3.3V (from controller)
              │
         Controller Button
              │
    ──────────┴──────────  Normal button contact
              │
         Optocoupler    ◄── PIC GPIO controls this
              │
             GND
```

### Pros:
- **Completely silent**
- **Instant response** (<1ms)
- **No mechanical wear**
- **Cheapest** - just optocouplers ($0.50 each)
- **No mounting/alignment issues**

### Cons:
- Requires opening and modifying the controller
- Need to trace PCB for button contacts
- Less "cool factor" than a mechanical robot

### Parts Needed:
| Item | Quantity | Cost |
|------|----------|------|
| PC817 optocouplers | 8 | $2 |
| Resistors (330Ω) | 8 | $0.50 |
| Wire | - | $1 |
| **Total** | | **~$4** |

---

## Option 4: Hybrid Approach

- **Electronic bypass** for frets + strum (speed + silence critical)
- **Servo** for whammy (needs analog position)
- **Servo or small motor** for tilt (occasional use)

This gives you:
- Silent note playing
- Still physically actuates whammy bar
- Working tilt for star power

---

## My Recommendation

**If noise is a concern, go with electronic bypass for the buttons.**

It's actually simpler than mechanical actuation:
- No mounting brackets to design
- No force/alignment calibration
- No solenoid power supply concerns
- Faster response time
- Cheaper

The tradeoff is you need to do some soldering inside the guitar controller, but it's not complex - just 7 pairs of wires (5 frets + 2 strum).

Would you like me to update the spec for an electronic bypass approach? I can also create a guide for mapping the PS2 guitar controller PCB.

_**Agent (claude-4.5-opus-high-thinking)**_

Understood - full mechanical actuation. Here are the best options for **quiet but fast mechanical** button pressing:

## Quiet Mechanical Actuator Options

### Option 1: Dampened Solenoids (Easiest)

Keep solenoids but reduce noise with physical dampening:

```
┌─────────────────────────────────┐
│      Solenoid with Dampening    │
│                                 │
│   ┌─────────┐                   │
│   │ Coil    │══╪══► [Rubber]──► Button
│   │ Body    │  │     pad         │
│   └────┬────┘  │                 │
│        │    Foam sleeve          │
│   [Rubber feet]                  │
└─────────────────────────────────┘
```

**Dampening techniques:**
- Rubber/silicone pad on plunger tip (soft landing)
- Foam sleeve around solenoid body (absorbs vibration)
- Rubber grommets on mounting (isolates from frame)
- Slower release (add small capacitor to slow de-energize)

**Noise reduction:** ~50-70%
**Added cost:** ~$1-2 per solenoid
**Speed impact:** Minimal (adds ~2-5ms)

---

### Option 2: Voice Coil Actuators

Speaker-like linear motors - push/pull without mechanical contact.

```
     ┌──────────────────┐
     │   ══════════     │  ← Permanent magnet
     │   ┌──────┐       │
     │   │ Coil │───────┼──► Pushrod to button
     │   └──────┘       │
     │   ══════════     │  ← Permanent magnet  
     └──────────────────┘
```

**Pros:**
- Very quiet (no impact)
- Fast (5-10ms)
- Proportional control possible

**Cons:**
- Need current control (H-bridge per actuator)
- Harder to source ready-made
- More expensive ($15-30 each)
- May need custom mounting

**Sources:**
- BEI Kimco voice coils
- Salvage from HDDs (small, may lack force)
- AliExpress "voice coil linear actuator"

---

### Option 3: Linear Servo Actuators

Small servos modified for linear push/pull motion.

**Examples:**
- Actuonix PQ12 ($30-50) - 20mm stroke, ~50ms cycle
- Firgelli L12 ($40-60) - configurable stroke/speed

```
┌────────────────────────┐
│  Actuonix PQ12         │
│  ┌────┐                │
│  │Motor├───[Screw]───► Pushrod
│  └────┘                │
│  20mm stroke, 50ms     │
└────────────────────────┘
```

**Pros:**
- Quiet (motor whine only)
- Position feedback available
- Easy to control (PWM like servo)

**Cons:**
- Slower (50-100ms cycle)
- Expensive ($30-50 each × 7 = $210-350!)
- **Too slow for Expert difficulty**

---

### Option 4: DC Motor + Cam Mechanism

Small DC motor spins a cam that pushes/releases a lever.

```
         Motor
           │
        ┌──┴──┐
        │ Cam │ ──► Pushes lever ──► Button
        └─────┘
           ↻
```

**Pros:**
- Quiet (just motor spin)
- Can be fast with proper gearing
- Cheap motors ($2-3 each)

**Cons:**
- Complex mechanism design
- Harder to control precise timing
- Need position sensing or timing calibration
- More parts to 3D print/fabricate

---

### Option 5: Piezoelectric with Lever (Advanced)

Piezo stack actuator with mechanical amplification.

```
     ┌───────────────┐
     │ Piezo Stack   │──┐
     └───────────────┘  │
                        ▼
              ┌─────────────┐
              │  Lever arm  │──► 5-10x amplified motion
              │  (fulcrum)  │
              └─────────────┘
```

**Pros:**
- Extremely fast (<1ms)
- Silent
- Precise

**Cons:**
- Very expensive ($50-200 each)
- Small displacement needs amplification
- High voltage drive (100-200V)
- Overkill complexity

---

## Recommendation: Dampened Solenoids

For your project, **dampened solenoids** offer the best balance:

| Factor | Rating |
|--------|--------|
| Speed | Excellent (12-25ms with dampening) |
| Noise | Acceptable (soft thud vs loud click) |
| Cost | Low (~$5-7 per actuator) |
| Complexity | Low |
| Expert capable | Yes |

### Dampening Kit Per Solenoid:

| Item | Purpose | Cost |
|------|---------|------|
| Silicone bumper pad | Soft landing on button | $0.25 |
| Foam sleeve | Absorbs body vibration | $0.30 |
| Rubber grommets (×2) | Mounting isolation | $0.20 |
| **Total per solenoid** | | **~$0.75** |

### Sound Comparison:

| Setup | Noise Level |
|-------|-------------|
| Bare solenoid | **CLICK CLICK CLICK** (annoying) |
| Dampened solenoid | *thup thup thup* (acceptable) |
| Voice coil | *whoosh* (quiet) |
| Servo | *whirr* (quiet hum) |

Stepper motors are an interesting option! Let me analyze their suitability:

## Stepper Motor Analysis

### Speed Calculation

For button pressing, you need minimal rotation (10-30°) with a lever arm:

```
                    Stepper Motor
                         │
                    ┌────┴────┐
                    │  Shaft  │
                    │   ○─────┼──► Lever arm ──► Button
                    │         │
                    └─────────┘
                    Rotate 15-30° to press
```

| Motor Size | Steps/Rev | For 30° (1/12 rev) | At 2000 step/s |
|------------|-----------|-------------------|----------------|
| NEMA 8 | 200 | ~17 steps | **8ms** |
| NEMA 11 | 200 | ~17 steps | **8ms** |
| With 1/8 microstep | 1600 | ~133 steps | **67ms** |

**Full steps = faster but louder, microstepping = smoother but slower**

---

## Stepper Pros & Cons for This Project

| Pros | Cons |
|------|------|
| Precise position control | Need lever/cam mechanism |
| Relatively quiet (with microstepping) | More complex wiring (4 wires each) |
| No impact noise at end of travel | Need driver IC per motor (or shared) |
| Can "hold" position | Slower than solenoids in full-step |
| Common, easy to source | 7 motors + drivers = more parts |
| Good torque at low speed | Power consumption when holding |

---

## Speed Comparison

| Actuator | Press Time | Release Time | Full Cycle |
|----------|------------|--------------|------------|
| Solenoid | 10-15ms | 10-15ms | **20-30ms** |
| Stepper (full step) | 8-15ms | 8-15ms | **16-30ms** |
| Stepper (microstep) | 30-70ms | 30-70ms | **60-140ms** |
| RC Servo | 40-80ms | 40-80ms | **80-160ms** |

**Steppers in full-step mode are competitive with solenoids!**

---

## Noise Comparison

| Mode | Noise Character |
|------|-----------------|
| Solenoid | CLICK (impact) |
| Stepper full-step | Buzzy/raspy stepping sound |
| Stepper 1/8 microstep | Smooth whirr |
| Stepper 1/16+ microstep | Near silent hum |

**Microstepping trades speed for smoothness/quiet**

---

### Per Button (×7):

| Component | Options | Cost |
|-----------|---------|------|
| Stepper motor | NEMA 8 or small 28BYJ-48 geared | $3-8 |
| Driver | A4988, DRV8825, or ULN2003 | $1-3 |
| Lever arm | 3D printed | ~$0.50 |

### Driver Options:

**Option A: Individual A4988/DRV8825 drivers**
```
PIC ──► A4988 ──► Stepper 1
    ──► A4988 ──► Stepper 2
    ... (×7)
```
- 2 pins per motor (STEP + DIR)
- 14 GPIO pins needed (PIC18F4550 can handle this)

**Option B: Shared driver board**
- TB6600 or similar multi-axis driver
- More complex, overkill for this

## Recommended Stepper Setup

### Motor: 28BYJ-48 (geared, 5V)

- Very common, cheap (~$2-3)
- Built-in 64:1 gear ratio
- Quiet operation
- 5V compatible (easy with PIC)

**But: SLOW** - gearing makes it ~15-25ms per step at output
- Too slow for fast Expert play

### Motor: NEMA 8 or Small Direct-Drive

- 20mm body, 200 steps/rev
- No gearing = full speed
- ~$5-8 each

```
NEMA 8 stepper (20x20mm)
     ┌─────┐
     │     │
     │  ○──┼──► 10mm lever arm ──► 3mm button travel
     │     │    (30° rotation gives ~5mm travel)
     └─────┘
```

---

## Wiring with PIC18F4550

The PIC18F4550 has enough pins, but it's tight:

| Function | Pins Needed |
|----------|-------------|
| 7 steppers (STEP+DIR) | 14 |
| Whammy servo (PWM) | 1 |
| Tilt servo (PWM) | 1 |
| UART TX/RX | 2 |
| USB | 2 |
| **Total** | **20** |

PIC18F4550 has ~35 I/O pins - **this fits!**

---

## My Assessment

| Criteria | Solenoid | Stepper (full-step) |
|----------|----------|---------------------|
| Speed | Excellent | Good |
| Noise | Loud click | Buzzy but softer |
| Cost (×7) | ~$35 | ~$50-70 |
| Complexity | Simple | Medium |
| Expert capable | Yes | Yes (with full-step) |
| Wiring | 7 wires + drivers | 14 wires + 7 drivers |
| Power | Spiky (pulse) | Steady (holding current) |

**Steppers are viable if you use full-step mode with a lever mechanism.**

---

## If Going With Steppers:

I'd recommend:
- **NEMA 8 steppers** (20mm, 200 step, bipolar) × 7
- **A4988 drivers** × 7 (or 2× quad driver boards)
- **Short lever arms** (10-15mm, 3D printed)
- **Full-step mode** for speed, accept some motor buzz

Pneumatics is actually a legitimate option! Let me break it down:

## Pneumatic System Overview

```
┌─────────────┐    ┌───────────┐    ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────────┐
│ Air Source  │───►│ Regulator │───►│ Manifold │───►│ Solenoid     │

│  or tank)   │    │           │    │  air)    │    │              │
└─────────────┘    └───────────┘    └──────────┘    └──────┬───────┘
                                                          │
                                          ┌───────────────┴────────────┐
                                          ▼                            ▼
                                   ┌─────────────┐              ┌─────────────┐
                                   │ Air Cylinder│              │ Air Cylinder│
                                   │ (presses    │   ... ×7     │ (strum)     │
                                   │  fret)      │              │             │
                                   └─────────────┘              └─────────────┘
```

---

## Pneumatic Pros & Cons

| Pros | Cons |
|------|------|
| **Very fast** (5-15ms) | Need air supply (compressor/tank) |
| **Soft actuation** (cushion of air) | Compressor is **LOUD** |
| **Adjustable force** (change PSI) | More complex plumbing |
| **Quiet at actuator** (puff vs click) | Higher initial cost |
| **Industrial reliable** | Potential air leaks |
| **Cool factor** | Overkill for 7 buttons? |

---

## Air Supply Options

### Option A: Small Compressor (Continuous)

| Type | Noise | Cost | Notes |
|------|-------|------|-------|
| Airbrush compressor | 50-60 dB | $50-100 | Quietest, 30-40 PSI |
| Pancake compressor | 70-80 dB | $80-150 | Louder, more capacity |
| Aquarium pump + tank | 40-50 dB | $30-50 | Very quiet, low pressure |

**Airbrush compressor** is the quietest option - designed for indoor use.

### Option B: Pre-Filled Tank (Silent Operation)

```
Fill tank beforehand ──► Use during play ──► Refill between sessions
```

- CO2 paintball tank ($30 + refills)
- Small air tank + hand pump
- **Completely silent during operation**

| Solenoid valves (×7) | Control air flow | $5-10 each |
| Mini air cylinders (×7) | Actuate buttons | $5-15 each |
| Tubing + fittings | Connect everything | $15-25 |
| **Total** | | **$150-250** |

## Noise Analysis

|--------|-------------|

| Air exhaust | Soft hiss (can muffle) |

**The actuators are quiet, but the compressor defeats the purpose if noise is your concern.**

### Quiet Pneumatic Setup:

1. **Pre-filled tank** (no compressor during play)
2. **Exhaust mufflers** on valves (reduce hiss)

| Adjustability | Fixed force | Adjust PSI |

## My Recommendation: Voice Coil Actuators

Voice coils are the sweet spot for your priorities:

```
┌────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│         Voice Coil Actuator                │
│                                            │
│    ┌─══════════════════════┐               │

│    └─══════════════════════┘               │
│                                            │
│  Current in coil → magnetic force → motion │
│  No mechanical contact = SILENT            │
└────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### Why Voice Coils are Cool:

1. **Same tech as speakers** - audiophile credibility
2. **Same tech as hard drive heads** - precision engineering
3. **Smooth, silent motion** - feels high-tech
4. **Proportional control** - can do soft press, hard press
5. **No click, no buzz** - just movement

```
- 5mm stroke
- 100g force  
- 5-12V operation
- ~$10-15 each
```

### Driver Circuit:

Voice coils need **bidirectional current control** (H-bridge):

```
PIC GPIO ──► PWM ──► Small H-Bridge ──► Voice Coil
                     (L9110S or similar)

Push: positive current
Pull: negative current (or spring return)
```

**L9110S module:** $1-2 for dual H-bridge, need 4 modules for 7 actuators

## Revised Recommendation

Given your priorities (quiet + cool + practical cost):

### Best Realistic Option: Well-Dampened Solenoids

With proper dampening, solenoids go from "annoying click" to "soft thud":

```
Noise reduction techniques:
├── Rubber tip on plunger (soft landing)
├── Foam sleeve on body (vibration absorption)  
├── Rubber grommets (mounting isolation)
├── Soft button contact (guitar button itself)
└── Enclosure (muffle remaining sound)

Expected result: 60-70% noise reduction
```

**Cost:** ~$50 total (solenoids + dampening materials)

---

### Alternative: Salvaged Hard Drive Voice Coils (Hacky Cool)

HDD actuators are voice coil, but **rotary** not linear:

```
     Pivot
       │
   ════╪════► Arm swings in arc
       │
    Magnet assembly
```

You'd need a linkage to convert arc to linear push. Complex but possible, and genuinely cool/unusual.

**Cost:** $0-20 (salvage drives) + mechanism design

## Ways to Make It Work

### 1. Mechanical Advantage (Lever)

```
        Voice coil pushes here (longer arm)
                   │
                   ▼
    ═══════════════╪═══════╗
                   │       ║
              Pivot●       ║
                   │       ▼
                   │    Button (shorter arm)
                   │       
               2:1 ratio = 2× force (half speed)
```

**Trade speed for force** - HDD actuators are very fast, you have margin to spare.

### 2. Use Larger/Older HDDs

Older enterprise 3.5" drives (15K RPM, server-grade) have beefier voice coils:
- Seagate Cheetah
- WD Raptor
- Enterprise SAS drives

These might produce 1-2N peak force.

### 3. Stack Multiple Magnets

Add external neodymium magnets to increase the magnetic field strength:

```
     [Added magnet]
          │
    ┌─────┴─────┐
    │  Voice    │ ← Stronger field = more force
    │   Coil    │
    └─────┬─────┘
          │
     [Added magnet]
```

Could boost force by 50-100%.

## Solenoid Physics Basics

Force in a solenoid (simplified):

```
         (N × I)² × μ₀ × A
F  ≈  ─────────────────────
              2 × g²

Where:
  N = number of turns
  I = current (amps)
  μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ (permeability of free space)
  A = core cross-sectional area (m²)
  g = air gap (m)
```

**Key insight:** Force increases dramatically as air gap decreases (inverse square). So a solenoid gets *stronger* as it pulls in.

---

## Proposed Design: Mini DIY Solenoid

### Physical Dimensions

```
         ┌─────────────────────────────┐
         │      Coil (wire wound)      │
         │  ┌─────────────────────┐    │
         │  │                     │    │
         │  │    ┌───────────┐    │    │
         │  │    │   Core    │════╪════► Plunger (moves)
         │  │    │  (fixed)  │    │    │   3-4mm stroke
         │  │    └───────────┘    │    │
         │  │                     │    │
         │  └─────────────────────┘    │
         └─────────────────────────────┘
         
         ◄──────── 15-20mm ───────────►
```

### Specifications

| Parameter | Value |
|-----------|-------|
| Core diameter | 4-5mm |
| Core material | Soft iron (nail, rod) or steel bolt |
| Coil length | 12-15mm |
| Coil outer diameter | 10-12mm |
| Wire gauge | 28 AWG magnet wire |
| Turns | 200-300 |

## Detailed Winding Calculation

### For 12V Operation:

**Target:** ~300mA for reasonable heat dissipation

**Resistance needed:** R = V/I = 12V / 0.3A = **40Ω**

**28 AWG magnet wire:**
- Diameter: 0.32mm (with enamel: ~0.35mm)
- Resistance: 0.213 Ω/meter

**Wire length needed:** 40Ω ÷ 0.213 Ω/m = **188 meters**

## Revised Design: Practical DIY Solenoid

Since we're pulsing (not continuous), we can run higher current for short durations.

### Design A: 12V, Higher Current, Fewer Turns

| Parameter | Value |
|-----------|-------|
| Voltage | 12V |
| Target current | 1A (pulsed, <100ms) |
| Resistance | 12Ω |
| Wire | 26 AWG (0.405mm, 0.134 Ω/m) |
| Wire length | 12Ω ÷ 0.134 = ~90m |
| Core diameter | 5mm |
| Coil ID | 5.5mm |
| Coil OD | ~15mm |
| Coil length | 15mm |
| Turns per layer | ~38 (15mm ÷ 0.4mm) |
| Layers | ~12-15 |
| Total turns | ~500 |

**Estimated force at 3mm gap:** ~40-60g ✓

---

### Design B: Simpler Build (Recommended)

Use thicker wire, fewer turns, rely on high pulse current:

| Parameter | Value |
|-----------|-------|
| Voltage | 12V |
| Wire | 24 AWG (0.51mm, 0.084 Ω/m) |
| Resistance | ~6Ω (allows 2A pulse) |
| Wire length | 6Ω ÷ 0.084 = ~71m |
| Core | M4 steel bolt (4mm) or 5mm iron rod |
| Coil length | 15mm |
| Turns per layer | ~29 |
| Layers | ~8 |
| Total turns | ~230 |
| Coil OD | ~13mm |

**Estimated force at 3mm gap:** 30-50g ✓

---

## Construction Guide

### Materials List (per solenoid)

| Item | Specification | Source | Cost |
|------|--------------|--------|------|
| Magnet wire | 24 AWG, ~75m per solenoid | Amazon/eBay | $10-15 for 200m spool |
| Core | M4×20mm steel bolt or 5mm iron rod | Hardware store | $0.20 |
| Plunger | M4 steel bolt (cut to length) or iron nail | Hardware store | $0.20 |
| Bobbin | 3D printed or plastic tube | - | $0.50 |
| Return spring | Small compression spring | Amazon/hardware | $0.10 |
| **Per solenoid** | | | **~$1-2** |

### Winding Steps

1. **Prepare bobbin:**
   ```
   3D print or use plastic tube
   ID: 5-6mm (for core)
   OD: ~8mm
   Length: 15-20mm
   Add flanges on ends to hold wire
   ```

2. **Insert core:**
   - Cut steel bolt/rod to ~25mm
   - Core stays fixed, plunger moves

3. **Wind coil:**
   ```
   Start at one end
   Wind tightly, layer by layer
   Keep tension consistent
   Count turns (aim for 200-250)
   Secure ends with tape or glue
   ```

4. **Add plunger:**
   - Separate iron/steel piece
   - Slightly smaller than bore
   - Attach pushrod for button actuation

5. **Add return spring:**
   - Small compression spring
   - Returns plunger when power off

- Surface field: ~0.3-0.5 Tesla

## Concept

```
         Key with neo magnet          UNPRESSED (4mm gap)
         ┌─────────────────┐
         │     [N][S]      │ ← Small neodymium magnet glued to key
         │      ↑↑↑        │
         └──────┼┼┼────────┘
                │││  4mm air gap
         ═══════╪╪╪════════════ PCB / mounting surface
                │││
         ┌──────┴┴┴────────┐
         │ Electromagnet   │ ← Coil with iron core
         │    (coil)       │
         └─────────────────┘


         Key pulled down             PRESSED (1mm gap)
         ┌─────────────────┐
         │     [N][S]      │ 
         └──────┼┼┼────────┘
                │││  1mm gap
         ═══════╪╪╪════════════
         ┌──────┴┴┴────────┐
         │ Electromagnet   │ ← Energized, attracts magnet
         └─────────────────┘
```

## Physics Analysis

### Force Between Electromagnet and Permanent Magnet

The force is approximately:

```
        B_coil × m_magnet × (dB/dx)
F  ≈  ─────────────────────────────
                  μ₀

Simplified for our case:
F  ≈  k × (N × I) × V_magnet × Br / g²

Where:
  N = coil turns
  I = current
  V_magnet = volume of neodymium magnet
  Br = remanence of neo magnet (~1.2T for N42)
  g = gap distance
  k = geometry factor (~0.5-2)
```

The force drops roughly as **1/g²** to **1/g³** depending on geometry.

---

## Design Calculation

### Small Neodymium Magnet

**Candidate: 4mm dia × 2mm thick N42 disc magnet**

| Property | Value |
|----------|-------|
| Diameter | 4mm |
| Thickness | 2mm |
| Grade | N42 |
| Surface field | ~0.4T |
| Pull force (to steel) | ~450g at contact |
| Pull force at 4mm | ~15-30g (estimated) |

### Electromagnet Coil

**Target: Generate enough field gradient to pull 50g at 4mm**

| Parameter | Value |
|-----------|-------|
| Core | Soft iron rod, 5mm dia |
| Coil ID | 6mm |
| Coil OD | 12mm |
| Coil length | 10mm |
| Wire | 28 AWG magnet wire |
| Turns | ~150-200 |
| Resistance | ~3-5Ω |
| Operating voltage | 12V |
| Current | ~2-3A |

---

## Estimated Force vs Gap

| Gap | Estimated Force | Notes |
|-----|-----------------|-------|
| 4mm (rest) | 20-40g | Just below trigger threshold |
| 3mm | 40-70g | Actuation begins |
| 2mm | 80-150g | Strong pull |
| 1mm | 200-400g | Very strong |
| Contact | 400-800g | Max (magnet touching core) |

**Key insight:** Once the magnet starts moving, force increases rapidly - this creates a "snap" action.

---

## Advantages of This Approach

| Advantage | Explanation |
|-----------|-------------|
| **Very quiet** | No plunger impact, magnet lands softly on key stop |
| **No moving parts in coil** | Just magnetic field, nothing mechanical |
| **Simple construction** | Coil + core, no springs or plungers |
| **Compact** | Electromagnet can be flat, PCB-mountable |
| **Fast response** | Magnetic force is instantaneous |
| **Reversible** | Reverse current = push instead of pull (if needed) |

---

## Challenges to Consider

| Challenge | Mitigation |
|-----------|------------|
| **Force at 4mm may be weak** | Use stronger neo magnet, more coil current |
| **Adjacent key interference** | Space coils adequately, use magnetic shielding |
| **Magnet alignment** | Ensure magnet centered over coil |
| **Key return** | Rely on keyboard switch spring (should be fine) |
| **Heat in coil** | Pulsed operation, adequate wire gauge |
| **Core residual magnetism** | Use soft iron (low coercivity) |

---

Before committing, test with:

### Materials (~$10)

|------|--------|------|

| Small iron bolt (M5×20) | Hardware store | $0.50 |
| 28 AWG magnet wire (small spool) | Amazon | $5 |

### Test Procedure

1. Wind ~150 turns around iron bolt
2. Attach neo magnet to a key or test weight
3. Position at 4mm above coil
4. Apply 12V, measure if it pulls
5. Add a scale to measure actual force

```
Test rig:

        ┌─────────────┐

        │    [N][S]   │ ← Neo magnet
        └──────┼──────┘

        ┌──────┴──────┐
        │    Coil     │
        │   on bolt   │
        └─────────────┘
               │
            12V supply
```

_**Agent (claude-4.5-opus-high-thinking)**_

<think><details><summary>Thought Process</summary>
The user is asking about a DIY voice coil actuator that could fit around a keyboard switch and pull on a custom keycap. This is an interesting idea - essentially making a linear voice coil motor that surrounds the switch.

A voice coil is essentially:
1. A permanent magnet (or magnets) creating a static magnetic field
2. A coil that moves within that field when current flows through it

The key difference from a solenoid:
- Solenoid: Coil is fixed, iron core/plunger moves (attracted by magnetic field)
- Voice coil: Magnets are fixed, coil moves (Lorentz force on current-carrying conductor in magnetic field)

For a keyboard switch:
- The switch body is typically ~15mm × 15mm × ~18mm tall
- We'd need a voice coil that surrounds it or sits next to it
- The coil would attach to the keycap and move up/down

Design concept:
- Ring-shaped magnet assembly around the switch
- Coil attached to keycap, sits in the magnetic field gap
- Current through coil pushes/pulls the keycap

This is similar to how some speakers work, but linear rather than conical.

Let me think about the physics:
- Force on a voice coil: F = B × L × I
  - B = magnetic field strength in the gap (T)
  - L = total length of wire in the field (m)
  - I = current (A)

For a reasonable force (50g = 0.5N):
- If B = 0.3T (achievable with neo magnets)
- And L = 5m of wire in the field (many turns)
- Then I = F / (B × L) = 0.5 / (0.3 × 5) = 0.33A

This is very achievable! And voice coils are inherently quiet because there's no iron core being attracted - just pure electromagnetic force on a conductor.


Now I should work through the actual construction details to see if this is feasible.</details></think>

## Voice Coil Physics

The force on a voice coil is:

```
F = B × L × I

Where:
  F = Force (Newtons)
  B = Magnetic field in gap (Tesla)
  L = Total wire length in the field (meters)
  I = Current (Amperes)
```

This is **linear with current** (unlike solenoids which are quadratic) - making it easier to control.

### Design Target

For 50g (0.5N) force:

| Parameter | Target | Notes |
|-----------|--------|-------|
| B (field) | 0.3-0.5 T | Achievable with neo magnets |
| L (wire in gap) | 2-5 m | Many coil turns in gap |
| I (current) | 0.3-0.8 A | Very reasonable |

## Component Design

### Magnet Assembly

**Configuration:** Dual opposing magnets creating radial field across gap

```
Top view:

              ┌─────────────┐
              │             │
         ┌────┤    Gap      ├────┐
         │ N  │  (coil      │ N  │
         │ ↓  │   here)     │ ↓  │
         │ S  │             │ S  │
         └────┤             ├────┘
              │   Switch    │
              │   (center)  │
              └─────────────┘
              
     Magnetic field lines go across gap:  N ──────► S
                                          ←──────
```

**Magnets:** 
- 4× N42 block magnets: 10mm × 5mm × 3mm
- Arranged in pairs on opposite sides
- Creates ~0.3-0.4T field in 3-4mm gap

### Voice Coil

**Design:** Rectangular coil that moves in the gap

| Parameter | Value |
|-----------|-------|
| Wire gauge | 30 AWG (0.25mm) |
| Turns | 50-80 |
| Coil width | 3mm (fits in gap) |
| Coil length | ~40mm (perimeter around switch) |
| Wire in gap | ~3-4m total |
| Resistance | ~3-5Ω |
| Operating current | 0.5-1A |

### Bobbin / Keycap Carrier

3D printed part that:
1. Holds the coil
2. Attaches to the switch stem
3. Supports custom keycap

## Detailed Specifications

### Force Calculation

```
Given:
  B = 0.35 T (neo magnets with steel yoke)
  L = 3.5 m (wire length in field)
  I = 0.7 A

Force = B × L × I
      = 0.35 × 3.5 × 0.7
      = 0.86 N
      = 87 grams ✓
```

**50g target is achievable with margin!**

### Electrical Specs

| Parameter | Value |
|-----------|-------|
| Coil resistance | 4Ω |
| Operating voltage | 5V |
| Operating current | 1.25A |
| Power | 6.25W peak |
| Force at 1.25A | ~100g |
| Force at 0.5A | ~40g |

### Mechanical Specs

| Parameter | Value |
|-----------|-------|
| Stroke | 4mm (keyboard switch travel) |
| Coil mass | ~2g |
| Response time | <5ms (very fast - low mass) |
| Resonant frequency | >100Hz |

```
    │  │     Steel Yoke       │   │ ─── 7. Steel plates (magnetic return)
    │  └──────────────────────┘   │
    └──────────────┬──────────────┘
                   │
        ┌──────────┴──────────┐
        │   Keyboard Switch   │ ─── 8. Standard MX switch
        └─────────────────────┘
```

### Step-by-Step Assembly

1. **Print housing and bobbin**
2. **Install magnets in housing** (careful - strong attraction!)
3. **Add steel yokes** (top and bottom of magnets)
4. **Wind coil on bobbin** (50-80 turns of 30 AWG)
5. **Attach bobbin to switch stem**
6. **Insert assembly into housing** (coil in gap)
7. **Connect coil wires to driver**

---

## Noise Analysis

### Why Voice Coils Are Quiet

| Factor | Solenoid | Voice Coil |
|--------|----------|------------|
| Moving mass | Heavy plunger | Light coil (~2g) |
| Impact at end | Hard stop | Soft (switch provides stop) |
| Magnetic attraction | Strong snap | None (force proportional to current) |
| Operation | Bang! | Smooth glide |

**Expected noise:** Near-silent. Only the keyboard switch click itself.

---

## Comparison: All Actuator Options

| Factor | Solenoid | Electromagnet+Neo | Voice Coil |
|--------|----------|-------------------|------------|
| Noise | Thud/click | Very quiet | **Quietest** |
| Force control | On/off | On/off | Proportional |
| Response | 10-20ms | 10-20ms | **<5ms** |
| Complexity | Medium | Medium | Higher |
| Cost (×7) | ~$38 | ~$26 | ~$27 |
| Cool factor | Medium | High | **Highest** |

---

## Advantages of Voice Coil Approach

1. **Quietest possible** - No plunger, no snap action
2. **Fastest response** - Low moving mass = quick acceleration
3. **Proportional force** - Can do soft/hard press
4. **Smooth motion** - No mechanical detents or catches
5. **No wear** - No rubbing parts (coil floats in air gap)
6. **Bidirectional** - Reverse current = push instead of pull
7. **Very cool** - Cutting-edge actuator technology

---

## Challenges

| Challenge | Mitigation |
|-----------|------------|
| Precision assembly | 3D print precise housing |
| Magnet alignment | Design with alignment features |
| Coil wire routing | Flexible leads, strain relief |
| Magnetic interference | Space switches adequately |
| Holding current | Low since no holding needed (switch spring returns) |

## How to Use

### Generate STL Files

```bash
# Install OpenSCAD first, then:
openscad -o bobbin.stl -D 'bobbin();' voice-coil-parts.scad
openscad -o housing.stl -D 'housing();' voice-coil-parts.scad
openscad -o wire-guide.stl -D 'wire_guide();' voice-coil-parts.scad
```

Or manually in OpenSCAD GUI:
1. Open `voice-coil-parts.scad`
2. Comment out `assembly();`
3. Uncomment the part you want (e.g., `bobbin();`)
4. Press F6 to render
5. File → Export as STL

### Print Settings

| Setting | Recommended |
|---------|-------------|
| Layer height | 0.15-0.2mm |
| Infill | 30-50% |
| Material | PLA or PETG |
| Supports | Yes (for housing magnet pockets) |
| Perimeters | 3 |

| `"assembly"` | All parts together (visualization only) |
| `"bobbin"` | Moving part - holds coil, attaches to switch stem |
| `"housing"` | Fixed part - holds magnets and yokes |
| `"wire_guide"` | Small strain relief clip |
| `"print_plate"` | All 3 printable parts arranged for batch printing |

Done! I've added comprehensive Wii guitar controller documentation to `SPEC.md`. Here's what was added:

## Updates to SPEC.md

### 1. Platform Options Section
Added comparison between PS2 and Wii platforms.

### 2. Wii Guitar Controller Reference Section
Complete protocol documentation from WiiBrew including:

**Controller Variants:**
- GH3 Gibson Les Paul (encrypted)
- GH World Tour (touchbar, different init)
- Third-party controllers

**Data Format (6 bytes):**
| Byte | Contents |
|------|----------|
| 0-1 | Analog stick X/Y |
| 2 | Touchbar (GHWT only) |
| 3 | Whammy bar (analog) |
| 4 | Strum Up/Down, +/- buttons |
| 5 | Fret buttons (G/R/Y/B/O), Pedal |

**Key Details:**
- Buttons are active LOW (0 = pressed)
- Extension connects to Wiimote (I²C protocol)
- Different initialization for GH3 vs GHWT guitars
- Touchbar values for GHWT guitars

### 3. Direct Interface Option
Documented the possibility of intercepting/emulating the Wii guitar protocol as a potential "Phase 5" experiment (though mechanical actuation remains the primary approach for the "cool factor").

### 4. Updated Sections
- System architecture diagram now shows "PS2 or Wii"
- Video capture section includes Wii connection
- BOM includes Wii Guitar + Wiimote option
- Open Questions includes platform decision
- References includes WiiBrew link

**Reference:** [WiiBrew - Guitar Hero Wii Guitars](https://wiibrew.org/wiki/Wiimote/Extension_Controllers/Guitar_Hero_(Wii)_Guitars)
